# Spectral Analysis

We did a spectral analysis back when analyzing series 2 as documented in
\[Data Overview S2.pdf\]. Unfortunately, the files on which that
analysis was performed were lost, and the analysis did not predict and
analyse what our averaging scheme would do to the spectrum of the
kinetic energy (used to estimate the temperature).

## Prediction

The kinetic energy recorded at each step is the average per particle
energy, or $E_k = \left( \sum_N v_i^2 \right) / 2N$, where $N$ is the
number of particles, $v_i$ is the is the velocity squared of particle
$i$, and the particle's mass is unity in scaled units. If the particles
were an ideal gas, their kinetic energy in each of the two dimensions
would be a Gaussian random variable with mean zero and variance equal to
the temperature. There will be $2N$ such random variables

```{r}
temp <-  0.015
N <- 256
simke <- function( N, t) sum((rnorm( 2 * N, mean = 0, 
                                        sd = sqrt( t))^2 / 2))
x <- replicate( 10000, simke( N, temp))
c(mean = mean(x), var = var(x))
```

The mean and variance are $n T$ (`r N * temp`) and $n T^2$
(`r N * temp^2`) respectively. Here is a histogram and associated
density.

```{r}
hist( x, 100, freq = FALSE)
xm <- N * temp; xsd <- sqrt( N * temp^2)
xi <- seq( from = -3 * xsd, to = 3 * xsd, by = xsd / 20) + xm
lines( xi, dnorm( xi, mean = xm, sd = xsd))
```

The kinetic energy per particle is that estimate divided by $N$.

```{r}
y <- x / 256
c( mean(y), sd( y))
```

This variance is $T/\sqrt{n}$ (`r temp/sqrt(N)`). To develop a
correlated set of 4M samples with a comparable spectrum, we would do
something like this.

```{r}
x <- rnorm( 4000000, mean = xm, sd = xsd) / 256
fl <- 200
filt <- rep( 1 / fl, fl)
# we have to drop the first fl -1 points as filter will return them as NA
y <- tail( stats::filter( x, filt, method = "convolution", sides = 1),
           -(fl - 1))
ps <- (-4500:4500) + 1000000 # move in 1M steps
plot( ps, y[ps - fl + 1], type = 'l', panel.first = grid())
#points( y[1:50+1000000])
```

That doesn't look right. Let's try an exponential filter.

```{r}
a <- 1 - (2 / (fl + 1)) # mimics the MA above
b <- 1 - a
z <- stats::filter( b * x, a, method = "recursive", init = x[1])

plot( ps,  z[ps], type = 'l', panel.first = grid(), main = "Exponential Avereage")
#points( z[1:500 + 1000000])
```

That's not quite right either. Let's look at the spectrums.

```{r}
qsdf( x, dt = 0.01, blocksize = 4096, panel.first = grid(), 
      normalize = TRUE, main = "Original Signal")
```

No correlation there.

```{r}
qsdf( y, dt = 0.01, blocksize = 4096, yrange = 60, panel.first = grid(), 
      normalize = TRUE, main = "Moving Avereage")
```

```{r}
qsdf( z, dt = 0.01, blocksize = 4096, yrange = 60, panel.first = grid(),
      normalize = TRUE, main = "Exponential Average")
```

So the spectrum from S2 in `Data Overview S2.nb.htlm` was more-or-less
flat topped at frequencies between $\pm 0.8/\tau$ and down 80 dB at at
$2.15\tau$. This would correspond to the $0.01\tau$ sample rate and a
Nyquist band of \[0, 50\]. The stop band would then be 0.08/50 or
`r 0.08/50`

```{r}
Fs <- 1/0.01
bo <- buttord( 0.8 / (Fs/2), 2.15 / (Fs/2), 10, 80)
bf <- butter( bo,  0.8 / (Fs/2), type = "low", plane = "z")
freqz( bf, fs = 1/0.01)
```

```{r}
v <- filter( bf, x)
plot(ps, v[ps], type = 'l', panel.first = grid(), main = "Butterworth")
```

```{r}
qsdf( v, dt = 0.01, blocksize = 4096, yrange = 110, normalize = TRUE)
```

The `rsmpavg()` function will perform a block average and re-sample the
signal with one sample for each block.

```{r}
rm( x, y, z)
rs <- rsmpavg( v, 500)
nps <- ps[seq( from = 250, to = 9000, by = 500)]
plot(ps, v[ps], type = 'l', panel.first = grid(), main = "Butterworth")
points(nps, rs[(nps / 500) - 1] )
```

The variable `rs` is now `r length( rs)`, so we can't do 4k FFTs.
`qsdf()` will default to 1K, which will be sufficient.

```{r}
qsdf( rs)
```

# Real Data

Below we read in `S5b.00150`, and plot the spectrum one-sided.

```{r}
x <- combineruns( td, "S5b", "00150", verbose = TRUE)
xsdf <- qsdf( tail(x$rundt$ke, -1000), dt = 0.0177737, blocksize = 4096, 
              yrange = 110, normalize = TRUE, panel.first = grid(), 
              main = "S5b.00150", spectype = "onesided")
```

The code below computes the frequency below which contains 99% of the
energy (plotted in @fig-S5b00150LL.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S5b00150LL
#| fig-cap: Log-Log plot of the spectrum, with the 99% energy line (blue) plotted (the red verticle line is the Nyquist frequency). The green line is the frequency response of the 500 point resample filter.  There is a verticle green line at the first null which will be the aliasing point (the Nyquist frequency of the resampled data).
xsdflin <- undB( xsdf$sdf[1:(length(xsdf$sdf)/2)]) # qsdf returns Decibels
xtp <- sum( xsdflin) # total power.
xsdfsum <- cumsum(xsdflin) / xtp
p99  <- which.max( xsdfsum > 0.99)
(freq <- xsdf$freqs[p99])
Fn <- 1/(2 * attr( xsdf, "dt"))
plot( xsdf, panel.first=grid(), xlim = c(xsdf$freqs[2], Fn), ylim = c( -60, 0),
      log = "x")
abline( v=freq, col='blue')
abline( v = Fn, col = "red")
abline( v = Fn/500, col = "green")
sincfreqs <- tail( c( seq( from = 0, to = freq, by = xsdf$freqs[2]/200), 
                xsdf$freqs[p99:length( xsdf$freqs)]), -1)
(function(x, n) lines( x, dB( abs(sin(pi*x*n/Fn)/(n*sin(pi*x/Fn)))), 
                       col="green"))(sincfreqs, 500)
```

The resapled data and its spectrum are below.

```{r}
rs <- rsmpavg( x$rundt$ke, 500)
nps <- seq( from = 250, to = length( x$rundt$ke), by = 500)
plot(x$rundt$ke, type = 'l', panel.first = grid(), main = "Resampled S5b.00150")
points(nps, rs, col = "red")
abline( v = 1000, col = "red")
abline( v = length( x$rundt$ke)/3, col = "blue")
```

The variable `rs` is now `r length( rs)`, so we can't do 4k FFTs.
`qsdf()` will default to 1K, which will be sufficient.

```{r}
qsdf( rs, blocksize = 128, main = "Resampled S5b.00150")
```
